chapter_theme: The decade of water-play (புனலாட்டுப் பத்து, marutham, Orampokiyar): the husband bathes in the river floods with another woman; the wife and her friend meet the gossip with charges (71, 75, 76, 79, 80), the man praises the woman of the water-play (72-74), and the rival invites him to the flood and away from his house (77, 78).

71.reading: The wife tells the lord of revels that people say he embraced his beloved, the woman of small fine bangles and bewitching sway, and bathed with her in the flood yesterday; such gossip can no more be hidden than the light of the sun can be buried.
71.nuance: The charge rests on what people say (என்ப), so the wife accuses him through the town's voice rather than her own sight; the sun image turns gossip into a force of nature that no one, least of all he, can stop. The two parallel questions (மறைத்தல் ஒல்லுமோ, புதைத்தல் ஒல்லுமோ) let the second answer the first.

thinai_evidence.note: the husband's bathing with another woman and the wife's charge are the field country's quarrel

comparisons.tenor: the gossip about his bathing with the other woman

72.reading: The man says that the soft, lovely woman, wearing a swaying leaf skirt of field water-lilies on her mottled waist, with swinging hair and kohl-lined eyes like the kuvalai, became his partner in the water-play when the flood came brimming with flowers.
72.nuance: The portrait runs from waist to hair to eyes before the verb arrives in the last line, so the woman is all ornament until she becomes a 'joined partner' (புணர்துணை). The poem never says whether she is his wife or another woman; set in this decade of charges about his bathing, his praise reads as his answer to them.

thinai_evidence.note: field water-lilies, the flower-laden flood and water-play belong to the watered fields

73.reading: The man says that when the bright-browed young woman in fine jewels leapt into the water-play, her bright-coloured leaf skirt swaying, the water of the great ford became cool and smelt of honeyed, fragrant kuvalai.
73.nuance: The hyperbole runs backwards from what one expects: the river does not cool or scent the woman; her leap gives the whole great ford her coolness and fragrance. The kuvalai is not said to grow there; the water simply smells of it once she is in it.

thinai_evidence.note: the kuvalai and the bathing ford of a river town are things of the fields

74.reading: The man says that the cool, fragrant hair of the woman who climbs the marutham tree on the bank and leaps into the water-play, her bright gold jewels glinting softly, is like the grace of a peacock gliding down from the sky.
74.nuance: The whole poem is one sentence that ends on the hair (கதுப்பே): the leap from the branch is seen through the spread of her hair as she falls, which is why the vehicle is a peacock descending rather than one dancing. The peacock is a bird of the hills brought into a field poem only as a simile.

thinai_evidence.note: the marutham tree on the river bank and the water-play place the scene in the fields

comparisons.tenor: her cool fragrant hair as she drops from the branch into the water

75.reading: The friend tells the lord of revels that because he is not one of the many here, the town has begun to gossip, its talk spreading wide: that she bathed with him in the cool water at the great ford of the ancient marutham tree.
75.nuance: Line 1 can be taken as praise (no one here is your equal, so you are watched) or as reproach (you do not fit among us); either way his standing is what turns a bath into news. மலர puns on அலர் in the same line: the gossip blooms like the flowers of the ford.

thinai_evidence.note: gossip about the husband's bathing with another woman is the field country's quarrel

76.reading: The speaker tells the man that the girl of bright bangles, with hair soft as panjaay sedge and freckles like fresh flowers, bathed with him in the cool water and grew in beauty until she looked like a goddess even to the women of the heavens.
76.nuance: The praise is the reproach: the other woman's beauty rose 'with you' (நின்னோடு), and the climb from earthly to heavenly comparison is pushed so far that it reads as mockery of his infatuation. பஞ்சாய் may also point to the sedge of which girls' dolls were made, so the hair would be a doll's hair.

thinai_evidence.note: the bathing pool and the waterside sedge belong to the fields; the quarrel is over his companion

comparisons.tenor: the pale spots on her skin
the girl after bathing with him

77.reading: The woman tells the lord of revels she has something to say: so that gossip rises through the great town, let us bathe with you in the cool water, tossed by its waves; come with us, do not go to your house.
77.nuance: Here the gossip that the wife and her friend dread in 71 and 75 is what the other woman wants: the public bath is meant to be seen. The last line sets 'with us' against 'your house' and makes the bath a choice between them.

thinai_evidence.note: the other woman drawing the husband from his house is the field country's quarrel

78.reading: The woman asks the man to bathe with her in the new flood that has burst its dam and come rushing down its course like the wall-breaking elephant of Killi, he of the leaf-bladed long spear and swift horses, and to take her shoulders as his raft.
78.nuance: A king's war elephant battering a fort wall is the image of a flood breaking a dam (சிறையழி), and the broken restraint carries over to the invitation itself. The speaker may also be the wife calling him back to her own water-play; the colophon gives no thurai to decide it.

thinai_evidence.note: a new flood breaking the dam of a watered field and bathing in it are things of the fields

comparisons.tenor: the new flood breaking its dam

79.reading: The woman tells the lord of revels, who seized her asking whose daughter this was, the girl whose eyes had reddened from bathing in the new flood: whoever's daughter she may be, who is he, whose son, to seize her without knowing?
79.nuance: She throws his own question back word for word (யார்மகள், யார் மகனை): a man who grabs women at the water without knowing their families has no family name worth asking about. If the speaker is the wife, the barb is sharper still: he did not know his own wife with her reddened eyes.

thinai_evidence.note: the husband's careless advance at the water-play and the woman's retort are the field country's quarrel

80.reading: The wife tells the lord of revels that she is not sulking and asks him to say truly why, after becoming the shoulder-companion of fine women and bathing in the red flood of the first rains, his eyes have turned so very red.
80.nuance: 'We are not sulking' opens a sulk. She offers the red, muddy first-rain flood as the reason for his red eyes and leaves him to deny the other reason, the women whose shoulders he held.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife's denied sulk over the husband's bath with other women is the field country's quarrel

links.note: Ainkurunuru 71: the wife says people report he bathed yesterday with his beloved (நெருநை ... ஆடினை என்ப), and the gossip can no more be hidden than sunlight. Akananuru 266: the wife opens with the same report (ஆடினை என்ப மகிழ்ந, நெருநை), compares the uproar to a victory feast, then says the gossip is no grief to her beside his broken oath.
links.teaches: The same reported charge, that he bathed with her yesterday, is the whole case in the Ainkurunuru but only the preface in the Akananuru, whose wife sets the gossip aside for the oath he broke, so the pair shows the bathing formula as a fixed opening of marutham complaint that a longer poem could push past to a deeper wrong.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 74: a young woman climbs the marutham tree on the bank and leaps into the water, her hair spreading like a descending peacock. Purananuru 243: an old man recalls how in youth he climbed the low marutham branch at the ford and leapt into the deep pool to the wonder of those on the bank.
links.teaches: The leap from the riverside marutham was a common game of youth in the field towns, and the two books use it oppositely: the akam poet freezes it as the height of a woman's beauty seen by a lover, while the puram poet, leaning on his staff, makes the same leap the measure of what age has taken.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 77: the other woman asks the husband to bathe with her so that gossip rises in the town, and not to go home. Kuruntokai 80: the courtesan says she will go to bathe at the flooded ford, and if the wife is afraid, let her guard her husband's chest with her kin like Ezhini's herds.
links.teaches: The Kuruntokai courtesan aims her dare at the wife, while the Ainkurunuru rival speaks to the man and names the gossip itself as her goal, so together they show the flood-bath as a public move in the rivalry, staged to be talked about and to pull him from his house, not a pleasure she hides.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 78: a woman asks the man to bathe in the dam-breaking flood, likened to Killi's wall-breaking elephant, and take her shoulders as his raft. Akananuru 312: the friend says that if the hill lord means to marry, they will bathe in the flood with his chest as their raft, and the lightning is likened to Vazhuthi's spear.
links.teaches: The raft of the lover's body runs in both directions: in the kurinji poem the girls take the man's chest as their float as the reward of a promised marriage, while in the marutham poem a woman offers her shoulders as his float to draw him away, and both dress the flood in a king's weapon, so the same intimate game and the same borrowed war image serve the making of a marriage in one land and its straining in the other.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 80: the wife asks why his eyes are so red after he bathed in the first-rain flood as the shoulder-companion of fine women. Naladiyar 387: the wife complains that the man who embraced other women comes to embrace her too without bathing.
links.teaches: In the Naladiyar the husband's fault is that he comes to his wife unwashed from other women, while in the Ainkurunuru the bath itself is the scene of his straying and its red eyes the evidence, so the pair shows bathing in the field country as both the cleansing a wife expects after his absence and the occasion of the absence.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 80: the wife asks why his eyes are red after bathing in the first-rain flood with fine women. Kalittokai 98: the husband says he was delayed bathing in the new flood of the Vaigai, and the wife turns the flood, point by point, into the woman he bathed with.
links.teaches: The Kalittokai shows the flood-bath as the husband's ready alibi and the wife unpicking it at length, while the Ainkurunuru wife grants the bath in a word and reads his red eyes as the trace of the women in it, so the pair shows the new flood as the standard excuse of the marutham husband and its marks on his body as the wife's standard proof.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 80: the wife, saying she is not sulking, reads his reddened eyes after the flood-bath as a sign of the women he bathed with. Kural 1313: the husband says that even if he wears a wreath of branch flowers, she grows angry, saying he wore it to show another woman.
links.teaches: Both turn the husband's body into evidence in a love-quarrel, but the Kural's husband protests that the sign is innocent and the suspicion hers, while the Ainkurunuru sign comes from a bath with women he did take, so together they show that the oodal's reading of marks on the man can be either jealous fancy or plain proof, and the couplet's comedy depends on the scene being the first.

source_issues: 71-80: the colophon has no thurai for this decade; speakers and addressees are inferred from the poems, so occasion words are null. In 72-74 no addressee is named and pira stands for that.
73 line 1: ஒந்தழை is probably a misprint for ஒண்தழை (bright leaf skirt); marked as printed.
73 line 4: புனவே is probably a misprint for புனலே (the water of the ford); marked as printed.
78 and 79: the speaker is not certain; 78 may be the wife rather than the other woman, and 79 may be the wife or another woman at the water.
